ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached circuit diagram shows an input voltage source Vi feeding a series resistor R1. After R1, the top node is connected to two parallel shunt branches: a Zener diode branch to the bottom return line and a load resistor RL branch to the same bottom return line. Thus, when the Zener is on, it clamps the load node voltage across RL. Given values: Zener breakdown voltage VZ = 20 V, maximum Zener current Iz(max) = 60 mA, R1 = 200 Ω, and RL = 1 kΩ. With the Zener on, the output/load voltage is clamped at 20 V. Therefore the load current is IL = VZ / RL = 20 V / 1000 Ω = 20 mA. The current through the series resistor is IR1 = (Vi - VZ) / R1 = (Vi - 20) / 200. For the Zener to just remain on, the resistor current must at least supply the load current: (Vi - 20) / 200 ≥ 20 mA. This gives Vi - 20 ≥ 4, so Vi ≥ 24 V. For the Zener current not to exceed its maximum rating, the resistor current must be no more than IL + Iz(max) = 20 mA + 60 mA = 80 mA. Thus (Vi - 20) / 200 ≤ 80 mA. This gives Vi - 20 ≤ 16, so Vi ≤ 36 V. Therefore, the input voltage range that maintains the Zener diode in the on state without exceeding its maximum current is 24 V to 36 V.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the Zener branch is in parallel with RL at the output node after R1. Remove the Zener and find the Thevenin equivalent seen by it. From the text, R1 = 200 ohm and RL = 1000 ohm, so Vth = Vi * RL/(R1 + RL) = Vi * 1000/1200 = 0.8333 Vi, and Rth = R1 || RL = 200 || 1000 = 166.7 ohm.
